st.headline: Singapore-based DayOne is said to pause US IPO plans on data centre, market concerns
st.teaser: Doubts about the potential payoff from massive investments into AI have fuelled volatility in global markets.
fullText: SINGAPORE – DayOne Data Centers has put plans for its multibillion-dollar US initial public offering on hold, sources familiar with the matter said, as investors question the sustainability of frothy valuations for digital infrastructure supporting the artificial intelligence boom.

The data centre operator, whose biggest customer is ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok, was initially intending to raise as much as US$5 billion (S$6.45 billion) from an IPO as soon as the fourth quarter, Bloomberg News reported previously.
But it started to reassess options including a delay or a smaller listing as volatility increased around data centres and AI stocks.
Singapore-based DayOne may still pursue an IPO in 2027 if the situation and market sentiment improves, the sources said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public.
The company filed for the IPO in October and has been working with Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup and BNP Paribas on the listing.
Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions on the IPO have been made, the sources said.
A representative for DayOne declined to comment.
Doubts about the potential payoff from massive investments into AI have fuelled volatility in global markets.
The Nasdaq 100 has dropped more than 6% in November, heading for its worst November performance since 2008.
Still, Anthropic staged a record-breaking US$107.3 billion IPO and private placement and rose 17% on its trading debut on Nov 19, becoming the world’s seventh-most valuable company.
Other data centre-related companies have either pulled or delayed their IPO plans amid investor concerns in the sector.

In October, Firmus Grid abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever initial public offerings, while Blackstone-backed AirTrunk is delaying a listing of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until 2027.

DayOne has hyperscale facilities in countries including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, which have seen a boom in data centre development, fuelled by demand from Chinese tech companies like ByteDance and Alibaba Group.

The US in November put interim rules on those four countries to restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips and servers, telling data centre operators they will need a license to purchase American tech hardware.
DayOne’s backers include Coatue, Hillhouse, GDS Holdings, SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

cna.headline: TikTok launches tool to help public figures detect deepfakes globally
cna.teaser: The "likeness detection tool" allows politicians and accounts with a large number of followers on TikTok to find and report AI-generated content using their image without consent.
fullText: LONDON: TikTok announced on Friday (Nov 20) the global launch of its deepfake-detection tool for public figures as the social media platform seeks to curb AI-generated disinformation ahead of a wave of European elections next year.

The "likeness detection tool" allows politicians and accounts with a large number of followers on TikTok to find and report AI-generated content using their image without consent, with the tool gradually being rolled out.
Deepfakes are text, images, videos and sounds that appear to be real but are generated or manipulated by AI.
For TikTok, owned by China-based ByteDance, the tool is a key part of protecting against disinformation during elections across Europe next year, including in Italy, France and Greece.
She added that the likeness tool would help "politicians and government identify potentially AI-generated content that has been shared potentially without their consent".
The European Union began rolling out sweeping artificial intelligence transparency rules in August, including a requirement for deepfakes and other AI-generated content to be labelled.
TikTok has required content creators to label realistic AI-generated images, audio and video for several years.
The company last year said that technological improvements would allow it to cut down on moderation jobs and locations worldwide.
AI has grown in importance for social media moderation as operators look to save money on human checks for content like pornography, misinformation and hate speech.
YouTube has also developed its own likeness detection tool to let creators detect AI-generated videos depicting their impersonators.
AFP, among more than a dozen other fact-checking organisations, is paid by TikTok in several countries to verify videos that potentially contain false information.

mom.headline: More than 782,000 Singaporean Seniors to Benefit from $1.04 Billion Budget 2026 CPF Top-Up to Boost Retirement Savings
mom.teaser: More than 782,000 eligible Singaporean seniors will receive a CPF top-up of up to $1,500 by 8 December 2026. First announced at Budget 2026, this top-up will support seniors who may face challenges in building their retirement savings.
